  ----------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: an engineer who has already drawn Gaussians and estimated a mean by sample average — no need to open on sigma-algebras.

**Empirical first**: a Monte Carlo estimator that is too noisy, a Metropolis chain that will not mix, a sampler that "works" in dim 2 and dies in dim 100. Only then do we name measure, Markov, Langevin.

Intractable expectations, complex laws, plausible data: from measure to Markov chains, Monte Carlo, MCMC, Langevin. Behind diffusion / score models: samplers and stochastic dynamics. This is the program's mathematical depth on the randomness side.

### What you will be able to do

-   Handle expectation and integration in the measure-theoretic sense (Tonelli-Fubini, conditional expectation) without loss of rigor.
-   State the convergence results (LLN, CLT, delta method) and use them to build confidence intervals by simulation.
-   Analyze a Markov chain: stationarity, reversibility, ergodicity, speed of convergence to the stationary distribution.
-   Implement the basic sampling methods: inverse, rejection, Box-Muller.
-   Build a Monte Carlo estimator and make it efficient: variance reduction, importance sampling.
-   Implement MCMC algorithms — Metropolis-Hastings, Gibbs — with the diagnostics that certify convergence, and use simulated annealing.
-   Connect Langevin dynamics to generative models: sample a high-dimensional density by following a stochastic process.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026-2027 catalog)

**Official objectives** (paraphrased from the description published on SynapseS): the course sets itself three objectives.

First, present the foundations of probability on the basis of abstract measure theory: construction of probability spaces, of probabilities on measured spaces and of integration over abstract spaces, with the essential properties of the integral.

Next, present and analyze Monte Carlo methods and their "Markov chain" version (MCMC). Finally, conclude with a brief introduction to generative models.

By the end of the course, a student can:

-   apply the fundamental concepts of probability theory and situate it within modern statistics, machine learning and applied contexts;
-   apply the basic Monte Carlo methods;
-   solve basic problems in machine learning and computational statistics that involve probability;
-   solve complex problems involving stochastic processes.

**Official syllabus "Plan for the Course"** (9 lectures) and mapping to our chapters:

### Where this course fits in the program

Elective of Year 1 · Period 1 (36 h, 4.5 ECTS), outside the recommended track: a choice of mathematical specialization rather than application.

The official description requires an undergraduate-level background in statistics, probability, linear algebra and calculus; for students of the X engineering cycle, the sheet additionally requires having taken at least one course among MAP432, MAP433.

In the master's program, its natural prerequisite is the [Refresher in Statistics](../m1p1-refresher-statistics/index.html) module, whose measure theory, random variables and convergence it takes up to raise them to the level required by simulation: the review chapter ensures the transition.

No Python prerequisite is required: the official sheet specifies that a mini-training and a tutorial are provided at the beginning of the course.

Downstream, three modules build directly on this course.

[Computational Optimal Transport for ML and Fairness](../m1p2-optimal-transport/index.html) draws on stochastic calculus and sampling for transport problems; [Multimodal Generative AI](../m1p2-multimodal-genai/index.html) revisits the score/diffusion family whose Langevin dynamics, in chapter 9, is one of the foundations; [Reinforcement Learning and Autonomous Agents](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html) builds on Markov chains and sampling (Monte Carlo methods for control and evaluation).

For students aiming at a PhD in applied probability or in generative modeling, it is the most formative P1 elective.

### Course outline

-   **Review: measure, random variables, convergence**: the foundation of the Refresher in Statistics, taken up at the theoretical level required afterwards.
-   **Measure and integration: expectation, Tonelli-Fubini**: constructing expectation properly and swapping limits and integrals safely.
-   **Convergence: LLN, CLT, delta method**: what simulation guarantees as the number of samples grows.
-   **Simulating: inverse, rejection, Box-Muller**: generating standard distributions, with their proofs and their limits.
-   **Monte Carlo and variance reduction**: estimating an integral by simulation, then making it converge faster.
-   **Importance sampling**: targeting the regions that matter to reduce the variance of an estimator.
-   **Conditional expectation**: the best possible prediction in the least-squares sense — a central object for generative modeling and for RL alike.
-   **Markov chains: stationarity, reversibility, ergodicity**: the theory underlying all the samplers in the course.
-   **MCMC: Metropolis-Hastings, Gibbs, diagnostics, annealing**: sampling intractable distributions, and knowing when the algorithm has converged.
-   **Langevin dynamics and generative models**: from the stochastic process to sampling high-dimensional densities — the gateway to score-based models.
-   **Research (Durmus): sampling in high dimension**: Alain Durmus's research on MCMC, Langevin, and generative modeling.

### Session plan {#sessions}

**36 h in class = 9 lectures of 2 h + 9 exercise sessions of 2 h.** The volume and its split are those of the SynapseS 2026–2027 sheet (official teaching methods: 9 lectures of 2 h and 9 exercise sessions of 2 h, some of them on laptop); the sheet gives the theme of each lecture but no chapter-level programme, so the assignment of chapters below is our proposal.

Each row is one week: a 2 h lecture followed by its 2 h exercise session.

Level 1 = foundations (reviews, definitions, first worked examples), 2 = core methods (Monte Carlo, conditioning, Markov chains, MCMC), 3 = advanced material (Langevin dynamics and its link with generative models); the level never goes down from one week to the next.
